questions.title: An induction that only closes once the hypothesis is strengthened
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.challenge_mechanism: The natural inductive hypothesis $S_n<\frac32$ is too weak to carry the step, because the step adds a strictly positive term; the student must notice this, construct the stronger statement $S_n\le\frac32-\frac1n$ whose tail absorbs the increment, and prove that stronger statement instead of the one asked for.
questions.question: For each integer $n\ge1$, let $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{k^{2}+1}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student tries to prove by induction that $S_n<\dfrac32$ for all $n\ge1$. Explain why the inductive step cannot succeed when the hypothesis is only $S_k<\dfrac32$, writing down the strongest inequality that the step actually gives.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prove by induction that $S_n\le\dfrac32-\dfrac1n$ for every integer $n\ge1$, and deduce that $S_n<\dfrac32$ for every integer $n\ge1$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the greatest real constant $c$ for which the inequality $S_n\le\dfrac32-\dfrac{c}{n}$ holds for every integer $n\ge1$, justifying your answer.

questions.answer:
**(a)** For $k\ge1$,
$$\frac{1}{k}-\frac{1}{k+1}=\frac{(k+1)-k}{k(k+1)}=\frac{1}{k(k+1)}.$$ **(M1)** Now $(k+1)^{2}+1=k^{2}+2k+2$ and $k(k+1)=k^{2}+k$, so $$(k+1)^{2}+1-k(k+1)=k+2>0,$$ hence $(k+1)^{2}+1>k(k+1)$ and therefore $$\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}<\frac{1}{k(k+1)}=\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}.$$ **(A1)(A1)** *(AG)*

**(b)** With the hypothesis $S_k<\frac32$ the step gives $$S_{k+1}=S_k+\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}<\frac32+\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}.$$ **(M1)(A1)** The right-hand side is strictly greater than $\frac32$ because $\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}>0$, so this does not establish $S_{k+1}<\frac32$. **(R1)** No rearrangement of a hypothesis of the form $S_k<\frac32$ can remove a positive increment, so the hypothesis has to be strengthened to one that leaves a gap larger than the increment. **(A1)**

**(c)** Claim: $S_n\le\frac32-\frac1n$ for all $n\ge1$. Base case $n=1$: $S_1=\frac12$ and $\frac32-1=\frac12$, so the claim holds, with equality. **(M1)** Inductive step: assume $S_k\le\frac32-\frac1k$. Then $$S_{k+1}=S_k+\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}\le\frac32-\frac1k+\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}.$$ **(M1)** By part (a), $\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}\le\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}$, so $$S_{k+1}\le\frac32-\frac1k+\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}=\frac32-\frac1{k+1}.$$ **(A1)** This is the claim with $n=k+1$, so by induction the claim holds for every $n\ge1$. **(A1)** *(AG)* Finally $\frac1n>0$, so $S_n\le\frac32-\frac1n<\frac32$ for every $n\ge1$. **(A1)**

**(d)** We want the largest $c$ with $S_n\le\frac32-\frac{c}{n}$ for all $n\ge1$. **(M1)** The case $n=1$ reads $\frac12\le\frac32-c$, that is $c\le1$, so no $c>1$ is admissible; part (c) shows that $c=1$ is admissible. **(A1)** Therefore the greatest such constant is $c=1$. **(A1)** For example, $c=\frac{3}{2}$ would demand $S_1\le0$, which is false because $S_1=\frac12$, so values above $1$ genuinely fail and the answer is not merely the largest value tested.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The **(M1)** is for combining the right-hand side into the single fraction $\frac{1}{k(k+1)}$; the two **(A1)** marks are for the comparison $(k+1)^{2}+1>k(k+1)$ and for concluding the inequality. A candidate who checks several values of $k$ without proving the general comparison earns at most **(M1)**: the point is the identity $(k+1)^{2}+1-k(k+1)=k+2>0$. Accept the equivalent form $\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}\le\frac{1}{k(k+1)}$ with no further work required.

(b) The step must be written out with the positive increment visible. Award **(M1)** for the decomposition $S_{k+1}=S_k+\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}$, **(A1)** for substituting the hypothesis, **(R1)** for observing that the resulting bound exceeds $\frac32$, and the final **(A1)** for the structural remark that a strictly positive increment cannot be absorbed by a bound with no slack. A candidate who writes only 'it does not work' with no inequality earns just the first two marks.

(c) The strengthened statement must be stated, not assumed. The base case is checked with equality, which is acceptable. Award **(M1)** for the base case, **(M1)** for the inductive hypothesis and the decomposition, **(A1)** for applying the inequality from (a), **(A1)** for the algebra reaching $\frac32-\frac1{k+1}$, and **(A1)** for the concluding deduction $S_n<\frac32$. Follow-through is allowed: a candidate who carries an incorrect constant from (a) but applies it consistently keeps the method marks.

(d) The base case gives $c\le1$ and part (c) gives admissibility at $c=1$. A candidate who simply states $c=1$ without the inequality $\frac12\le\frac32-c$ loses the **(M1)**. Condone a brief note that smaller values of $c$ give a weaker, hence also true, inequality; the question asks for the greatest constant.
questions.explanation:
Part (a) is a small algebraic fact, but it is the engine of the whole question: it is exactly the telescoping difference $\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}$, which is slightly larger than the increment $\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}$. The denominator $k^{2}+1$ was chosen so that $(k+1)^{2}+1=k^{2}+2k+2$ exceeds $k(k+1)=k^{2}+k$ by exactly $k+2$, giving the clean comparison. Had the denominator been $k^{2}$, the comparison would point the wrong way and the argument would need a different tail entirely.

Part (b) is the conceptual heart. Induction is usually presented as 'assume it for $k$, prove it for $k+1$', and students expect the hypothesis to be used verbatim. Here the hypothesis $S_k<\frac32$ gives $S_{k+1}<\frac32+\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}$, a bound that has moved the wrong way. The bound is not merely inconvenient: because the increment is strictly positive, no amount of algebra starting from $S_k<\frac32$ can produce $S_{k+1}<\frac32$. The only way forward is to prove something stronger, a statement with a margin that grows and can therefore absorb the increment.

Part (c) supplies that margin. The tail $-\frac1n$ is chosen so that the slack between consecutive values, $\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}$, is at least the increment; part (a) is precisely that statement. The base case holds with equality and the step preserves the bound, so the stronger claim is established. Part (d) pins the constant: the base case forces $c\le1$, so $c=1$ is the best possible tail of this shape, and larger constants fail immediately at $n=1$.

The classic wrong turns are: assuming the hypothesis $S_k<\frac32$ is enough and writing a circular step; treating the inequality in (a) as an equality; trying to prove the weaker $S_n<2$ instead, which is true but does not answer the question; and in (d) forgetting that the base case, not the step, is what bounds $c$ from above. A useful check is that $S_1=\frac12$ exactly, which is why the constant $\frac32$ and the tail $\frac1n$ meet at $n=1$.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the AHL 1.15 bullet on proof by mathematical induction. The design chooses a sum whose natural induction hypothesis is provably too weak, so the student must construct the stronger statement $S_n\le\frac32-\frac1n$ and then use it; the summand $1/(k^2+1)$, the constant $\frac32$, the tail $\frac1n$ and the final part pinning the greatest constant are all constructed here, and every value was checked by direct summation in exact rational arithmetic.

verification.method: Exact rational and numerical checks: the telescoping identity in (a) was verified for $k=1,\dots,8$; the base case and the strengthened bound $S_n\le\frac32-\frac1n$ were checked against direct summation for $n=1,\dots,10$; and the bound $c\le1$ from the base case together with the limiting value of $k(k+1)/((k+1)^2+1)\to1$ were verified numerically.

questions.title: The cubic whose odd symmetry is hidden by a translation
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: AHL 2.12 (polynomial functions, their graphs and equations), AHL 2.14 (odd and even functions)
questions.subtopic: 2.12 Polynomial functions and equations; 2.14 Odd and even functions
questions.challenge_mechanism: The symmetry is given only as the functional equation $f(2+t)+f(2-t)=4$, which is oddness about the point $(2,2)$ rather than about the origin; the student must first translate the origin and recognise an odd function before the odd/even structure can be used, and the remaining coefficient is then pinned by a repeated root instead of by any stated coefficient.
questions.question: The function $f$ is a cubic with leading coefficient $1$, and for all real $t$ it satisfies $$f(2+t)+f(2-t)=4.$$

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that $g(t)=f(2+t)-2$ is an odd function, and deduce that $f(x)=2+a(x-2)^{3}+b(x-2)$ for some real constants $a$ and $b$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given also that $f$ has a repeated root, determine the values of $a$ and $b$ and hence the equation of $f(x)$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence factorise $f(x)$ completely, state its roots, and determine the coordinates of its point of inflection.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the number of real solutions of $f(x)=k$ for each real value of $k$, using the symmetry and the turning points of the graph.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Put $g(t)=f(2+t)-2$. Then $$g(t)+g(-t)=\bigl(f(2+t)-2\bigr)+\bigl(f(2-t)-2\bigr)=4-4=0,$$ **(M1)** using the given condition with the same $t$. Hence $g(-t)=-g(t)$ for all real $t$, so $g$ is odd. **(A1)**

Since $f$ is a cubic, $g$ is a cubic in $t$. An odd polynomial contains only odd powers of $t$, so $g(t)=at^{3}+bt$ for constants $a$ and $b$. **(R1)** Writing $t=x-2$ gives $f(x)-2=a(x-2)^{3}+b(x-2)$, that is $$f(x)=2+a(x-2)^{3}+b(x-2).$$ **(A1)** *(AG)*

**(b)** The leading coefficient of $f$ is $1$, so $a=1$. **(A1)** With $y=x-2$, the equation $f(x)=0$ becomes $$y^{3}+by+2=0.$$ **(M1)** A cubic $y^{3}+py+q$ has a repeated root exactly when its discriminant $-4p^{3}-27q^{2}$ is zero. **(M1)** Here $p=b$ and $q=2$, so $-4b^{3}-108=0$, giving $b^{3}=-27$ and hence $b=-3$. **(A1)** Therefore $$f(x)=(x-2)^{3}-3(x-2)+2.$$ **(A1)** *(AG)*

**(c)** Expanding, $(x-2)^{3}=x^{3}-6x^{2}+12x-8$ and $-3(x-2)=-3x+6$, so $$f(x)=x^{3}-6x^{2}+9x=x\left(x^{2}-6x+9\right)=x(x-3)^{2}.$$ **(M1)(A1)** The roots are $x=0$ and the repeated root $x=3$. **(A1)** The point of inflection is the centre of symmetry $(2,2)$, since $f(2)=2$; equivalently $f''(x)=6x-12$ vanishes at $x=2$. **(A1)** As a check on the symmetry, the half-turn about $(2,2)$ carries the point $(0,0)$ to $(4,4)$, and indeed $f(4)=4$.

**(d)** Differentiating, $f'(x)=3x^{2}-12x+9=3(x-1)(x-3)$. **(M1)** Hence $f$ has a local maximum at $x=1$ with $f(1)=4$ and a local minimum at $x=3$ with $f(3)=0$. **(A1)** These are reflections of each other in the point of symmetry $(2,2)$, since $2\cdot2-1=3$ and $2\cdot2-4=0$. **(A1)** Reading the graph: for $k<0$ there is one solution; for $k=0$ there are two distinct solutions, $x=0$ and the repeated root $x=3$; for $0<k<4$ there are three solutions; for $k=4$ there are two distinct solutions; and for $k>4$ there is one solution. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The **(M1)** is for the translation $g(t)=f(2+t)-2$ and the addition of the two shifted equations; the **(A1)** is for recognising that $g(t)+g(-t)=0$ is precisely the definition of an odd function. The **(R1)** is for the statement that an odd polynomial has only odd powers, which is what converts oddness into the shape of $f$. A candidate who writes $f(x)=2+a(x-2)^3+b(x-2)^2+c(x-2)$ without eliminating the even powers has not used oddness and forfeits the **(R1)**. Accept $b$ in place of the linear coefficient; the names are not important.

(b) The **(A1)** for $a=1$ follows from the stated leading coefficient. The repeated-root condition must be converted into a condition on $b$: award **(M1)** for the substitution $y=x-2$ and **(M1)** for invoking the discriminant, then **(A1)** for $b=-3$ and **(A1)** for the assembled cubic. A candidate who instead sets $f(x)=(x-r)^{2}(x-s)$ and matches coefficients should be fully credited, since it reaches the same unique answer. Condone an unsimplified form of $f$.

(c) Accept any correct factorisation route, including division by $x$ after noticing the zero constant term. The point of inflection may be found from the symmetry given in the stem or from $f''(x)=0$; either is acceptable.

(d) The **(M1)** is for locating the turning points, the **(A1)** for their values, and the **(A1)** for linking them by the central symmetry. The final **(A1)** requires all five cases, including the degenerate values $k=0$ and $k=4$ where a double root reduces the number of distinct solutions; a candidate who gives three solutions at $k=0$ or $k=4$ loses the final mark.
questions.explanation:
The stem states the symmetry as a functional equation about the point $(2,2)$, not about the origin, and this is the whole difficulty. An even function satisfies $h(-x)=h(x)$ and an odd function satisfies $h(-x)=-h(x)$, but neither applies to $f$ directly. Subtracting the centre, $g(t)=f(2+t)-2$, moves the point of symmetry to the origin, and only then does the odd condition become usable. This construction is the step students skip: they look for odd or even powers of $x$ in $f$ and find none, because the symmetry lives in the translated variable $x-2$.

Once $g$ is known to be odd, the shape of $f$ is forced: a polynomial odd in $t$ has only odd powers, so $f(x)=2+a(x-2)^{3}+b(x-2)$. Part (b) then pins the coefficients. The leading coefficient fixes $a=1$, and the repeated root fixes $b$. The clean way to use the repeated root is the discriminant: after the substitution $y=x-2$, the equation is $y^{3}+by+2=0$, and its discriminant $-4b^{3}-108$ vanishes only at $b=-3$. There is no second value, so the cubic is unique.

Part (c) reveals why the numbers were chosen: the cubic factors as $x(x-3)^{2}$, so the repeated root sits at $x=3$ and the simple root at $x=0$, both consistent with the central symmetry about $(2,2)$, which swaps the point $(1,4)$ with $(3,0)$.

Part (d) is where the graph features matter. The local maximum and minimum are images of each other under the half-turn about $(2,2)$, so the horizontal lines $y=k$ cut the graph in a pattern symmetric about $k=2$. The subtle cases are $k=0$ and $k=4$, where the line passes through a turning point and the double root means only two distinct solutions. The classic wrong turns are treating the symmetry as being about $x=0$, forgetting that the repeated root gives a double but not a triple solution, and missing the degenerate counts at the turning-point values.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the AHL 2.12 bullet on polynomial graphs and equations and the AHL 2.14 bullet on odd and even functions. The design hides the symmetry in a translated variable, gives it as the functional equation $f(2+t)+f(2-t)=4$, and then pins the cubic by a repeated root through the discriminant rather than by a stated coefficient. The functional equation, the point $(2,2)$, the repeated root at $x=3$ and the five-case count in (d) are all constructed here, and every value was verified by substitution.

verification.method: Substitution and exact factorisation: the oddness of $g(t)=f(2+t)-2$ was checked for several $t$; the cubic $(x-2)^3-3(x-2)+2$ was expanded and evaluated at $x=0,1,2,3$; the discriminant condition $-4b^3-27q^2=0$ was checked at $b=-3$; and the solution counts of $f(x)=k$ were verified by sign changes of $f(x)-k$ at $x=0,1,3,4$.

questions.title: A compound-angle equation whose squared version invents solutions
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: AHL 3.10 (compound angle identities), AHL 3.11 (relationships between trigonometric functions)
questions.subtopic: 3.10 Compound angle identities; 3.11 Relationships between trigonometric functions
questions.challenge_mechanism: The equation must be rewritten with the compound-angle identity and then factorised, but the tempting route of squaring both sides produces the extra equation $\sin 2x(\sin 2x-1)=0$, so two roots that solve the squared equation but have the wrong sign must be identified and rejected.
questions.question: Consider the equation $$\cos 2x=\sqrt{2}\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right).$$

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that $\sqrt{2}\cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\cos x-\sin x$ and that $\cos 2x=(\cos x-\sin x)(\cos x+\sin x)$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence solve the equation $\cos 2x=\sqrt{2}\cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ for $0\le x<2\pi$, giving each answer as a multiple of $\pi$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student solves the equation by squaring both sides. Explain how this leads to $\sin 2x(\sin 2x-1)=0$, and identify the extraneous solutions that the squaring introduces.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the general solution of the equation, and hence the number of solutions that lie in the interval $-2\pi\le x\le2\pi$.

questions.answer:
**(a)** By the compound-angle formula, $$\sqrt{2}\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\sqrt2\left(\cos x\cos\frac{\pi}{4}-\sin x\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\sqrt2\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}(\cos x-\sin x)=\cos x-\sin x.$$ **(M1)(A1)** Also, by the double-angle formula and the difference of two squares, $$\cos 2x=\cos^{2}x-\sin^{2}x=(\cos x-\sin x)(\cos x+\sin x).$$ **(A1)** *(AG)*

**(b)** Substituting the results of (a), $$(\cos x-\sin x)(\cos x+\sin x)=\cos x-\sin x,$$ so $$(\cos x-\sin x)\bigl(\cos x+\sin x-1\bigr)=0.$$ **(M1)**

Case 1: $\cos x=\sin x$, that is $\tan x=1$, giving $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$ or $x=\frac{5\pi}{4}$ in $[0,2\pi)$. **(A1)**

Case 2: $\cos x+\sin x=1$. Writing the left side as $\sqrt2\cos\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ gives $\cos\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so $x-\frac{\pi}{4}=\pm\frac{\pi}{4}+2k\pi$. **(M1)** Hence $x=0$ or $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ in $[0,2\pi)$. **(A1)**

The solutions are $x=0$, $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$, $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi}{4}$.

**(c)** Squaring both sides gives $\cos^{2}2x=2\cos^{2}\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$. **(M1)** Using $\cos^{2}2x=1-\sin^{2}2x$ and $2\cos^{2}\theta=1+\cos2\theta$ with $\theta=x+\frac{\pi}{4}$, the right-hand side is $$1+\cos\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=1-\sin2x.$$ **(A1)** Hence $1-\sin^{2}2x=1-\sin2x$, that is $\sin^{2}2x=\sin2x$, or $$\sin2x\,(\sin2x-1)=0.$$ **(A1)**

The squared equation therefore admits $x=0,\frac{\pi}{2},\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2}$ from $\sin2x=0$ and $x=\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4}$ from $\sin2x=1$. **(A1)** Of these, $x=\pi$ and $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$ do not solve the original equation: at $x=\pi$ the left side is $1$ and the right side is $-1$, while at $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$ the left side is $-1$ and the right side is $1$. They are extraneous and must be rejected.

**(d)** From (b), $\cos x=\sin x$ gives $x=\frac{\pi}{4}+k\pi$ for $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. **(M1)** Also $\cos x+\sin x=1$ gives $x=2k\pi$ or $x=\frac{\pi}{2}+2k\pi$ for $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. **(A1)**

In $[-2\pi,2\pi]$ the family $\frac{\pi}{4}+k\pi$ contributes $k=-2,-1,0,1$, that is $-\frac{7\pi}{4},-\frac{3\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4}$, four values; the family $2k\pi$ contributes $-2\pi,0,2\pi$, three values; and the family $\frac{\pi}{2}+2k\pi$ contributes $-\frac{3\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}$, two values. **(M1)** These nine values are all distinct, so there are $9$ solutions. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The **(M1)** is for the compound-angle expansion and the **(A1)** for evaluating $\cos\frac{\pi}{4}=\sin\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$; the second **(A1)** is for the double-angle factorisation. A candidate who quotes $\cos2x=1-2\sin^{2}x$ instead of the factorised form has not produced the factor needed in (b), so the second **(A1)** should not be given unless the factorisation is also shown.

(b) The **(M1)** is for setting the two expressions equal and factorising. A candidate who divides by $(\cos x-\sin x)$ and so loses $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi}{4}$ forfeits the first **(A1)**. The second case needs the compound-angle rewrite $\cos x+\sin x=\sqrt2\cos\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$; award **(M1)** for this and **(A1)** for the two roots. Accept any order of the four solutions.

(c) All four marks depend on the algebra being shown. The **(A1)** for $2\cos^{2}\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=1-\sin2x$ requires the double-angle identity applied with the correct angle; a common slip is to write $\cos\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ instead of $\cos\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$. The final **(A1)** requires the two extraneous values to be named and tested against the original equation; merely saying that squaring can introduce roots earns nothing.

(d) The general solutions must carry the $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ parameter; accept $\tan x=1$ written as $x=\frac{\pi}{4}+k\pi$. The count of $9$ is earned only if the three families are enumerated over the closed interval. A candidate who takes the four solutions of (b) and doubles them, or who omits the endpoints $x=-2\pi$ and $x=2\pi$, loses the final **(A1)**.
questions.explanation:
The equation is dressed in a compound angle, and the first move is to expand $\sqrt2\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ with the compound-angle identity. That expansion is not cosmetic: it produces $\cos x-\sin x$, which is exactly the factor that $\cos2x$ contains by the difference of two squares. The whole equation therefore becomes $(\cos x-\sin x)(\cos x+\sin x)=(\cos x-\sin x)$, and factorising reduces it to two simple cases. This is the structural reason that $\sqrt2$ and $\frac{\pi}{4}$ appear together: they are chosen so that the compound-angle expansion matches the double-angle factorisation.

The first trap is the common factor $\cos x-\sin x$. Dividing by it discards the two solutions where it vanishes, $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi}{4}$. Factorising keeps them. This is the standard error in this family of equations, and part (b) is arranged so that a careless cancellation still yields two of the four answers, which makes the mistake easy to miss.

Part (c) exposes a second trap, squaring. Squaring both sides is superficially attractive because both $\cos2x$ and $\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ invite a double-angle identity. It does give a solvable equation, $\sin2x(\sin2x-1)=0$, but squaring is not reversible and enlarges the solution set. The two values $x=\pi$ and $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$ solve the squared equation because the two sides have equal magnitude there but opposite signs, so the residual is $\pm2$ rather than $0$. Identifying and testing these is the point of the part.

Part (d) asks for the general solution and then counts over a closed interval of length $4\pi$. The three families $\frac{\pi}{4}+k\pi$, $2k\pi$ and $\frac{\pi}{2}+2k\pi$ must each be enumerated; both endpoints $x=\pm2\pi$ belong to the second family, so omitting either loses a solution. The classic wrong turns are cancelling the common factor, accepting the roots introduced by squaring, and forgetting either the parameter $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ or the closed endpoints.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the AHL 3.10 bullet on compound angle identities and the AHL 3.11 bullet on relationships between trigonometric functions. The design chooses a constant and an angle so that the compound-angle expansion reproduces the double-angle factor of $\cos2x$, then uses the resulting common factor and a squaring step as two separate traps; the equation, the extraneous roots and the nine-value count are all constructed here, and every solution and residual was verified numerically.

verification.method: Numerical verification: the compound-angle identity was checked at several $x$; the four solutions of (b) and the four values of the general families were substituted into the original equation with residual zero; the two extraneous values $x=\pi$ and $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$ were shown to have residuals $2$ and $-2$; the squaring identities were checked numerically; and the three families were enumerated over $[-2\pi,2\pi]$ to give $4+3+2=9$ distinct solutions.
